name: PT Sarana Meditama Metropolitan Tbk

frontmatter.title: PT Sarana Meditama Metropolitan Tbk — valuation reflects required capacity, indexed-out konglo premium
frontmatter.summary:
SAME runs 8 EMC hospitals around Jakarta with 1,428 licensed beds at 48.1%
occupancy. Two forces set value: a post‑pandemic outpatient rebound met by the 2025 capacity build, and the
konglo regime — 79.0% EMTEK control, free float 14.2%, HSC status
and the FTSE Russell deletion from 21 December 2026. Fundamental value Rp124; konglo‑lens
target Rp210; rating REDUCE.
thesis: Revenue grows 10% in FY2026E to IDR2,048.2bn, anchored on nine-month revenue of IDR1,532.0bn rather than a haircut to it [S3,S4].

EBITDA of IDR369.7bn is struck on total nature-of-expense D&A of IDR254.0bn — roughly three times the depreciation line in the data pack — so the EV/EBITDA cross-check uses the real charge [S3,S0]. Capex falls to 7% of revenue in FY2026E and rebuilds to 12% [S3,S4].

Nine-month EBIT fell to IDR88.0bn from IDR94.6bn on the prior year as costs outran revenue [S4]; the forecast anchors operating cost at the nine-month actual and earns margin back only as the 2025 capacity matures [S3,S4].

The konglo lens closes only 35% of a 2.1x price‑to‑current‑value gap in the base regime — only the dated regime catalysts (HSC exclusion, FTSE‑Russell deletion, MSCI review) can improve convergence [S5,S6].

catalysts.event: FTSE Russell removes SAME and other Indonesian HSC‑list micro caps from its global indices
MSCI decision on whether to move Indonesia from Emerging to Standalone status (opened 15 October 2026)

blocks.text: **REDUCE. Price Rp236. Target Rp210. Return -11.1%.** The fundamental twelve‑month value is Rp124 from a DCF that restates D&A to the LK’s total nature-of-expense charge of IDR254.0bn — fixed assets plus right-of-use plus intangibles, roughly three times the depreciation line the data pack carries — and includes the stepped‑up stake in PT Nitrasanata Dharma (JEC, listed July 2026) [S3,S4]. The 2.1x price‑to‑current‑value gap is a regime variable, not a valuation input: the lens keeps it, closing only 35% in the base regime, after the HSC and FTSE‑Russell deletions slow the compress curve [S5,S6].

The target reflects **two paths** — hospital operations fighting the medical‑trend rate the company itself flags for 2026 [S3] but supported by the 2025 capacity additions [S3], and the Indonesia‑specific konglo regime that prices the stock on missing float flow rather than on those operations [S5,S6].

Indonesian private hospitals compete for a patient book split between the state‑run JKN, insurers’ managed‑care
panels, and cash payers. The KRIS standard‑class inpatient tariff caps that took effect in 2025 stop the historical
pass‑through of imported‑drug and device cost‑push.

Our base case starts from the **nine-month actual** — revenue of IDR1,532.0bn, operating cost at 23.6% of revenue and EBIT of IDR88.0bn against IDR94.6bn a year earlier [S4] — and grows revenue 10% in FY2026E to IDR2,048.2bn. Growth tapers from 10% in FY2026E to 7% by FY2030E as the 1,428‑bed base fills from 48.1% occupancy [S3]. Gross margin holds at 29.4% because procurement scale offsets the medical trend; capex falls to 7% of revenue in FY2026E and rebuilds to 12% by FY2030E as replacement spending returns [S3,S4]. Terminal growth is the house 5% to avoid assuming cost inflation is a pricing‑power story. The liquidity discount is the template 20%, applied after the konglo lens.

What moves the value: **occupancy** (each point of the 1,428‑bed base filled lifts revenue without new fixed cost) competes with **the capex cycle** (IDR472.0bn at its peak in the last forecast year). The konglo path is set: HSC exclusion from the IHSG (effective 13 November 2026) and the FTSE‑Russell deletion (21 December 2026) are booked [S5,S6]; the MSCI review on 30 June 2027 is the next test. As a konglo name, the valuation does not hinge on the operations alone but on the float — the reason we publish.

SAME — PT Sarana Meditama Metropolitan Tbk — operates the EMC Healthcare hospital network: 8 hospitals clustered in Jakarta and its eastern and southern corridors, with 1,428 licensed beds and a weighted occupancy rate of 48.1% in FY2025 [S3]. The network admitted 57,096 inpatient visits and served 729,578 outpatient visits in FY2025, at an average length of stay of 3.2 days [S3]. Consolidated revenue was IDR1,862.0bn against COGS of IDR1,309.4bn, and the company reports a single hospital-operations segment [S0,S3].

Revenue by service line in FY2025: medical support — pharmacy, laboratory and radiology — at IDR1,097.6bn, inpatient rooms and operating and delivery theatres at IDR440.0bn, outpatient at IDR150.7bn, administration at IDR80.0bn and other hospital services at IDR93.7bn [S3]. Read together, the mix says what kind of hospital company this is: the majority of the rupiah is earned on diagnostics, drugs and procedures ordered around a stay, not on the room itself. That makes volume per bed, case mix and the prescriber base the operating levers, and it makes the doctor roster — not the building — the scarce asset.

**Ownership and group.** EMTEK holds 79.0% of SAME directly; the company is the group's healthcare platform and describes itself as supported by EMTEK's investment commitment [S3]. SAME was built into a network through the acquisitions of PT Elang Medika Corpora and PT Kedoya Adyaraya, and management states it now manages 8 hospitals [S3]. The group also holds 34.0% of PT Nitrasanata Dharma, the Jakarta Eye Center operator that listed in July 2026 and is carried as an associate [S4]. That stake matters twice: it is a second, eye-care growth engine outside the hospital bed count, and it is a related-party asset whose value the market can now mark daily.

**Strategy.** The 2025 capital programme was explicitly technology-led rather than bed-led: the Sentul expansion was completed and inaugurated, renovation and refurbishment ran across several units, a Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT scanner was installed at Grha Kedoya, and robotic surgery was added at Alam Sutera, with the Tangerang Royal Suites among the capacity additions [S3]. Management frames this as differentiating on clinical capability and patient journey in "an increasingly competitive and complex hospital industry landscape" [S3]. The economics of that choice are visible in the accounts: a heavier fixed-asset base and a depreciation charge the data pack understates, which the financials section restates.

**Market position.** SAME is a challenger, not the leader: it competes in the Jakarta private-hospital market against larger listed networks and against standalone private hospitals, and its 1,428-bed base at 48.1% occupancy leaves room to grow revenue without new buildings [S3]. Its differentiation is premium diagnostics and tertiary capability in a market where the state insurer pays a capped tariff, so the commercial book — private insurance and self-pay — carries the margin. The company does not disclose its payer split with enough precision to model it directly; we treat it as a risk factor rather than a forecast input and discuss the regulatory direction in the industry section [S3,S7].

Indonesian private hospitals earn from a tripartite patient book: the state JKN scheme, insurer
managed-care panels, and self-payers. Consolidation among listed operators has been slow because hospital
licences, doctor privileges and referral networks are local, so scale advantages show up in procurement and
in payer negotiation rather than in pricing power over patients.

**Demand backdrop.** Indonesia's economy expanded at a steady pace in 2025 with consumer price inflation inside Bank Indonesia's target band, and the annual report frames the hospital industry against that stable macroeconomy [S3]. Demand for private hospital care is a function of formal-sector employment and insurance coverage rather than of GDP alone: the state JKN scheme widens the pool of insured patients while capping what each episode pays, and the private-insurance and self-pay books carry the margin. For a premium-positioned operator such as EMC, the relevant market is therefore the insured urban middle class in Jakarta and its satellite cities — the corridor where all 8 of its hospitals sit [S3].

**Regulation is the dominant industry driver, and it runs against tariff-led growth.** The board's own governance commentary names "growing regulatory complexity, including the implementation of the Standard Inpatient Class (KRIS) under BPJS Kesehatan and the obligation to integrate healthcare service data" as a central risk it monitors [S3]. The KRIS rules reshape the physical product of a BPJS ward — reported limits of a maximum of two beds in the top class and four in the lower classes [S7] — which forces capital spending on ward configuration and, at the same time, caps the room-rate revenue that spending can earn back. Separately, the Ministry of Health has been pushing hospitals to compete on clinical competence and technology rather than on bed counts [S8]. Read together, the two policies point the same way: beds are no longer the unit of growth; capability, case mix and outpatient throughput are. That is precisely the strategy SAME executed in 2025 with the PET/CT scanner, robotic surgery and the Sentul and Tangerang capacity additions [S3].

**Competitive structure.** The Jakarta private-hospital market is fragmented: listed networks, group-owned hospitals and independent private hospitals compete for the same consultants and the same insured patients, and no operator holds a share large enough to set price. SAME is a challenger with 1,428 beds at 48.1% occupancy [S3]; its route to share is tertiary capability that smaller independents cannot fund, and its constraint is that those capabilities require the depreciation base discussed in the financials section. Supply-side power sits with importers of drugs and devices, whose prices move with the rupiah; buyer-side power sits with BPJS as a monopsonist and with insurer panels that negotiate case rates. The result is a business where cost discipline and procurement scale — not price — decide margin, which is why the model holds gross margin near the last actual rather than assuming tariff-driven expansion [S3].

**Industry-level flow shock.** The sector's market pricing is currently set less by these operating facts than by the ownership-concentration regime: the exchange expanded its high-shareholding-concentration list to several hundred names and excluded them from the IHSG calculation from 13 November 2026 [S5], and FTSE Russell deleted the Indonesian names in that cohort from its global indices effective 21 December 2026 [S6]. SAME sits inside that cohort. The industry consequence is that even a well-run hospital operator with a small float trades on index mechanics: passive demand disappears, the marginal buyer is a domestic retail investor, and the discount to fundamental value persists until ownership structure changes. We treat that as an industry-level externality in the valuation rather than as a company-specific fault.

Hospital economics are unusually local. A hospital's catchment is a drive-time radius, its referral base is a
set of named physicians with admitting privileges, and its licence is issued against a bed count and a service
classification. That is why hospital consolidation has historically delivered less scale benefit than in
industrials, and why operators defend share through consultant relationships and equipment rather than
through price.

**History.** Revenue compounded from IDR1,393.5bn in FY2022A to IDR1,862.0bn in FY2025A, with gross profit of IDR552.6bn and a gross margin of 29.7% [S0,S3]. Operating cost of IDR437.6bn, D&A included, leaves EBIT of IDR115.7bn and an EBIT margin of 6.2% [S3]. The difference between that and EBITDA of IDR369.7bn is total D&A from the LK nature-of-expense note: fixed-asset depreciation of 254.0bn for FY2025 and 232.4bn for FY2024, plus right-of-use depreciation and intangible amortisation of 21.9bn on the next line of the same note [S3,F6,F21]. This is the correction the report makes. The data pack's D&A line is roughly a third of that charge, and because EBIT already deducts the intangible amortisation while capex already includes intangible additions, carrying only the fixed-asset line as the add-back understates free cash flow to the firm by the amortisation every year. We restate revenue, EBIT, net profit and both years of total D&A as facts, so the engine rebuilds history and the LTM from the filing: FY2025A EBITDA is 19.9% of revenue on the full charge, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on that figure rather than on the pack's [S3,S0]. On the DCF leg the corrected add-back is worth about seven rupiah a share before the operating-cost anchor offsets it; the valuation section carries the arithmetic.

**Where the profit goes.** Interest expense of IDR71.6bn absorbs most of EBIT; net profit attributable to shareholders was IDR30.1bn, a net margin of 1.6% and a return on equity of 0.8% on equity of IDR3,801.2bn [S0,S3]. That is the honest picture of the franchise: the asset base was revalued and expanded faster than earnings, so book value is large relative to profit and the equity story rests on future utilisation, not on current returns. Net debt of IDR825.7bn is 2.2x EBITDA and cash was IDR152.4bn at year-end [S0,S3].

**Cash flow and capex.** FY2025 capex of IDR348.4bn — 18.7% of revenue — funded the Sentul extension, the Tangerang Royal Suites, the PET/CT scanner and robotic surgery [S3]. Free cash flow to the firm was only IDR39.7bn, which is the central tension in the model: growth is real but it is bought with cash. Our forecast cuts capex to 7% of revenue in FY2026E and lets it build to 12% by FY2030E and 13% by the last forecast year as the announced additions reach their replacement cycle, rather than repeating the FY2025 peak; the nine-month filing shows fixed-asset and intangible additions already far below that pace [S4]. Working capital is small — 2.1% of revenue — because patient and insurer receivables are short-dated and payables fund the drug and consumable book [S0,S3].

**Forecast.** We grow revenue 10% in FY2026E, anchored on the nine-month filing where revenue and gross profit both ran above the prior-year period at a gross margin slightly below the full-year FY2025 level [S4], then fade to 7% as the 1,428-bed base fills from 48.1% occupancy [S3]. The nine-month actual carries the warning the forecast has to answer: EBIT of IDR88.0bn against IDR94.6bn a year earlier — down about seven per cent while revenue rose — because selling and administrative costs outran the top line [S4]. We therefore anchor the FY2026E operating-cost ratio at the nine-month actual of 23.6% and earn back only 22.8% by FY2030E as the 2025 capacity matures: the FY2026E EBIT step is a cost-efficiency step on a flat margin, not a revenue one [S3,S4]. Gross margin is held at 29.4% to 29.7% — the last actual level plus procurement benefit, no margin expansion story [S3]. EBITDA margin lands near 19.4% in FY2026E and 19.5% by FY2035E; capex rises to IDR472.0bn in the last forecast year, 13% of revenue against terminal total D&A of 13%, so the terminal year runs at total-D&A parity [engine].

**Capital allocation and earnings quality.** The company pays no dividend — DPS of 0.00 and a payout ratio of 0.0% — so all capital is retained into beds and equipment [S0]. Our screen flags three things. First, cash conversion: net profit of IDR30.1bn against FCFF of IDR39.7bn means earnings are not yet cash, and the accruals gap closes only if capex falls as we model. Second, the D&A restatement above: the pack's depreciation line is roughly a third of the total charge, so any valuation built on it both understates EBITDA and, through the missing amortisation add-back, understates free cash flow; we rebuild both from that note and hold terminal capex at total-D&A parity. Third, related-party exposure is modest — 0.0% of revenue — but the associate stake of 34.0% in PT Nitrasanata Dharma is a group-linked asset we value explicitly rather than assume away [S3,S4]. The IDX regime flags (HSC status, free float below the regulatory minimum, index deletions) are governance rather than accounting issues and are handled in the governance section [S5,S6].

**Method set.** A hospital operator is a long-lived, capital-intensive, largely domestic cash-flow business with a regulated revenue cap, so discounted free cash flow to the firm is the primary method at 70% of the blend [S0,S3]. EV/EBITDA is a cross-check at 30%, applied to the restated last-actual EBITDA the engine rebuilds from the filing, not to the data pack's LTM. The peer set is frozen in the assumptions file at this report's date — the nine listed hospital operators with a usable EV/EBITDA — so the 12.4x median can be reproduced from a named list rather than a peer universe that grows during the session [S0]. We do not use a P/E cross-check: the reported net profit is small relative to the asset base, the trailing multiple is 134.6x on a 1.6% net margin, and a P/BV cross-check would be distorted by the PSAK 16 land revaluation in book value, so neither tells us anything the cash flow does not [S3]. The 34.0% stake in PT Nitrasanata Dharma is valued explicitly rather than double counted: the LK carries it at 849.4bn [S4], while our covered sibling JECX is a SELL whose house fundamental is below that carrying value and the market price is above it. Because the sibling is covered in this house, the stake is marked to the house fundamental pre-lens, not to book or to market, and that mark is the single bridge item in the model [S4,F23].

The cost of capital is 10.6%. The cost of equity is 11.7%, built as a risk-free rate of 7.4% less the house sovereign default spread of 1.6% (the IDR curve already carries that spread, so it is deducted rather than added), plus a levered beta of 0.9x — from an unlevered 0.7x and gearing of 32.0% — on a mature-market premium of 4.2% plus a country risk premium of 2.5%, and no company-specific premium of 0.0%: the risks we can name are in the cash flows and the konglo overlay, not in the discount rate. Debt enters at 9.4% pre-tax, the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread, at 24.3% of the structure; the model charges actual interest at the drawn HSBC rate of 8% (JIBOR plus the facility margin), which is lower than the new-issue rate the WACC uses, so the discount rate is the conservative one of the two and the two are not additive [S0,S3].

The DCF values the equity at Rp99 per share on an enterprise value of IDR2,506.5bn, of which 56.7% is terminal value — a terminal share we accept because a hospital network with a licence, a bed base and a referral book is a perpetual asset, but one we test below. The terminal year is struck with capex at 13% of revenue, the same as terminal total D&A of 13%, so the terminal year is a maintenance year: the 5% terminal growth is served by filling the existing 1,428-bed base from 48.1% occupancy rather than by net new capital, which is why the terminal reinvestment rate is low and the incremental return on it is above the WACC even though the average return on the revalued asset base is not. The EV/EBITDA cross-check, at 12.4x on the restated last-actual EBITDA of IDR369.7bn, gives Rp220, 122.6% away from the DCF [S0,S3]. That divergence runs the other way from a floor: the sector multiple is high because peers are priced on EBITDA before the capex a hospital network needs to keep earning, and our cash flow charges for that capex. We keep the cross-check because it shows what a trade buyer would pay, but we let the cash-flow value lead; the multiple is applied to last-actual EBITDA in every scenario, so the operating scenarios move the DCF leg only.

**The D&A correction, per share.** Two corrections offset on the DCF leg. Restating the add-back to total nature-of-expense D&A puts the 21.9bn intangible amortisation back into free cash flow to the firm every year — worth about seven rupiah a share on the DCF leg before the operating-cost change — while anchoring FY2026E operating cost at the nine-month actual takes back about eight. The two together leave the published target within a rupiah or two of where it stood before this round; the substance of the correction is that the EBITDA base, and therefore the cross-check, is now on the real charge rather than two-thirds of it.

**The konglo lens.** Fundamental value is Rp124. The stock trades at Rp236. The 2.1x ratio the lens reports is price over Rp111, the current-year method-weighted value; measured against the twelve-month fundamental of Rp124 it is a little under two times, and the lens does its work on the current-year measure so the roll is not counted twice [S5,S6]. Under the house konglo framework that premium is a regime variable, not an operating one: it exists because 79.0% of the shares are held by EMTEK and the free float is 14.2%, below the exchange's 15.0% minimum, so the marginal price is set by a thin pool of domestic buyers rather than by the cash flows [S5]. The lens asks how much of that gap closes over the next twelve months. In the base regime it closes 35% of it, giving a konglo target of Rp203 before the HSC overlay; the overlay adds 5%, and the published target is Rp210 [S5,S6]. In the bear regime 75% of the gap closes; in the bull regime the premium widens rather than compresses, at -10%. We then apply the template liquidity discount of 20%.

**What the price implies.** The reverse DCF holds today's price and solves for the growth that would justify it: the market is paying for FY2027E revenue growth of 18.5% against the 9.5% our forecast delivers [engine]. The gap is a growth-rate gap, not a margin one — the price needs roughly double the growth we can source from the bed base — and the konglo premium is the only thing bridging it [S0]. That is why the rating is REDUCE with a target of Rp210 and a total return of -11.1%: we are not short the hospital, we are short the premium, and the catalyst that would close it is an ownership or index event, not an earnings event [S5,S6].
**Risk register (likelihood × impact).**

*Regulatory — high likelihood, high impact.* KRIS standard inpatient class and the data-integration mandate are named by the board itself as growing regulatory complexity [S3], and the reported ward rules cap beds per class in the state-insured segment [S7]. If private-class tariffs are compressed alongside public ones, the revenue per admission assumption fails and gross margin, not volume, takes the hit. The Ministry's push toward competence- and technology-based hospital classification cuts the other way for EMC — it rewards the capability investment already made — but it also raises the capital bar for staying in the premium tier [S8].

*Operating and tariff — medium-to-high likelihood, high impact.* The 2025 build (Sentul extension, Tangerang Royal Suites, PET/CT, robotic surgery) lands fixed costs ahead of utilisation at 48.1% occupancy [S3]. Medical trend running ahead of what payers will reimburse is the most likely operating failure, and it hits revenue per admission as well as volume: the bear case cuts growth and gross margin together rather than treating the tariff as a volume-only risk.

*Financial — medium likelihood, medium impact.* Net debt is 2.2x EBITDA and interest expense of IDR71.6bn consumed most of FY2025 EBIT of IDR115.7bn [S0,S3]. A rupiah move raises both imported drug and device costs and the cost of the floating portion of that debt, so FX and funding risk arrive together.

*Konglo and liquidity — high likelihood, medium impact.* Free float is 14.2%, 0.8% short of the 15.0% exchange minimum — a gap of less than one percentage point, not a chasm [S25]. The 31 March 2029 compliance date is the deadline for the market-cap tier SAME sits in (market cap IDR4,050.9bn [S0]); issuers above the tier threshold face the earlier deadline that runs from 2027 [S25], so a re-rating of the shares would shorten the clock rather than lengthen it. SAME was removed from the IHSG calculation with the high-concentration cohort from 13 November 2026 and is named in FTSE Russell's December 2026 deletion list, effective 21 December 2026 [S5,S6]. Passive flow is leaving; a rights issue, a controller sell-down or a group placement to restore float is the plausible fix, and each changes the per-share math in a different direction.

*Governance and related parties — low likelihood of manipulation, medium impact.* Related-party revenue is 0.0% of the total and the 34.0% stake in PT Nitrasanata Dharma is a group-linked associate [S3,S4]. We found no fabricated-cash or fictitious-revenue flag in our screen; the exposures we carry are structural (control, float, associate valuation), not accounting fraud.

**The group agenda is the second upside.** EMTEK took control with roughly seventy-two per cent of the shares in November 2020 and injected all but a rounding fraction of PT Elang Medika Corpora, which brought EMC Tangerang and EMC Sentul into the company, in August 2021 — the documented precedent for SAME as the group's healthcare platform [S3]. The konglo card names asset injections and placements as the modal re-rating driver, and here the group has both a reason and a deadline: the float must reach 15.0% by 31 March 2029, and the cheapest way for a controller to do that without selling down is to inject assets for shares or place stock to a strategic holder [S25]. We do not put that in the base case — there is no announced plan, no filing and no date — but it is in the bull narrative and it is a dated watch item, because a group asset injection at book would lift the per-share value while a discounted private placement to an affiliate would dilute it [S3,S25].

**Scenarios, mirrored.** We shock the same two drivers in opposite directions and give the base case a majority weight: probabilities of 45% base, 30% bear and 25% bull. The bear case carries the largest single downside weight because medical-trend compression is the risk we rate highest, and it cuts growth and gross margin together - a revenue-per-admission shock as well as a volume one; the bull case is the exact mirror, with faster fill of the 2025 additions and a procurement-led gross margin gain, on the assumption KRIS is implemented without a private-class tariff cut. Both are published in the assumptions file, and neither touches the multiple, which stays on last-actual EBITDA. On the pre-konglo values that yields Rp100 / Rp151 / Rp230; after the konglo lens, Rp150 / Rp203 / Rp284. Note the asymmetry the lens imposes: even the bear operating case is supported by a partial premium, and the bull case assumes the premium persists.

**The konglo lens on the risk.** The price is 2.1x the current-year weighted value and a little under twice the twelve-month fundamental [S5,S6]. Over twelve months the base regime closes 35% of that gap, the bear 75%, and in the bull the premium widens by -10%. The regime flags that decide which happens are dated, not speculative: the FTSE Russell deletion on 21 December 2026 [S6], the exchange's quarterly HSC review and the 15.0% free-float deadline [S5]. A regime where the controller adds float or the index treatment normalises compresses the premium faster than any earnings surprise; a regime where it does not leaves the stock expensive on fundamentals and cheap on nothing.

**Signposts that would change our view.** Occupancy crossing the mid-fifties without new beds; gross margin holding through a KRIS tariff announcement; a float increase above the regulatory minimum; a JEC dividend/consolidation decision; and any change in the HSC list at the quarterly review [S3,S5].

**Ownership and control.** EMTEK holds 79.0% of SAME directly and treats the company as its healthcare platform, funding the network's investment programme [S3]. The free float is 14.2%, 0.8% below the 15.0% minimum, and the compliance ladder runs to 31 March 2029 for the market-cap tier SAME currently sits in [S25]. The ownership numbers do not add up cleanly and we say so: EMTEK's direct 79.0% leaves a fifth of the shares outside the controller, yet the registry's insider measure is 89.0% and its free float is 14.2%, which together exceed the share count [S0]. The difference is definitional — the insider block counts affiliates, MESOP shares and directors that the free-float measure treats as float — and we cannot reconcile the block from the filings we hold, so we flag it to the Director as a registry gap rather than paper over it. For a minority holder the governance fact stands either way: the controller can fund growth, and it also sets the price of the shares by deciding when and how float is created.

**Regime flags.** SAME is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list (as of 11 November 2026), which removed it from the IHSG calculation from 13 November 2026, and it is named among the Indonesian names FTSE Russell deletes from its global indices effective 21 December 2026 [S5,S6]. These are disclosure and index actions, not findings of wrongdoing; the konglo registry carries no enforcement action against the company. The investment consequence is mechanical: fewer index-tracking buyers, a thinner marginal price, and a premium to fundamental value that we treat as a regime variable [S5]. The lens that prices it is set out in the valuation section: the 2.1x ratio is price over the current-year weighted value Rp111, and a little under twice the twelve-month fundamental Rp124 — the measure we would defend if the regime normalised [S5,S6].

**Related parties and structure.** Revenue from related parties is 0.0% of the total — low by IDX standards — while the 34.0% stake in PT Nitrasanata Dharma is a group-linked associate carried at 849.4bn, which we mark to the house fundamental in the valuation bridge [S3,S4]. On pledges we searched the 2025 annual report and the Q3 2026 consolidated filing for pledge language ("gadai", "diagunkan", "dijaminkan") and found no disclosure of a pledged controlling stake; the konglo registry carries no pledge field at all, so the negative is checked-but-thin and we report the missing registry field to the Director rather than claim a clean bill [S3,S4]. No auditor change: the FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion from Purwanto Susanti dan Surja (EY) dated 24 March 2026 [S3].

**Dividend and capital allocation.** No dividend is paid (DPS 0.00, payout 0.0%); capital is retained into beds, equipment and the associate stake [S0]. For a minority investor that is a governance choice as much as a financial one, and it is why the return has to come from the share price rather than from cash yield.

**ESG.** The material exposures are clinical: patient safety and clinical governance, hospital waste and infectious-material handling, and the KRIS ward-standard and health-data-integration obligations the board names as regulatory complexity [S3,S7]. The company reports community programmes around its Sentul hospital and BPJS service awards, which we read as evidence of operating engagement rather than as a differentiated ESG profile [S3]. Labour is the other exposure: a hospital network's cost base is clinicians, and attrition in a competitive Jakarta market is a real constraint on the growth plan [S3].

**Dated catalysts.** 21 December 2026 — FTSE Russell deletion takes effect, the flow event we can date [S6]; every quarter — the exchange's HSC review, where a change in status would move the regime [S5]; FY2026 results — the first full year that tests whether the 2025 capacity earns its depreciation [S3,S4]; and the free-float ladder, where the 31 March 2029 date applies to the current market-cap tier while the earlier 2027 deadline would bite on a re-rating [S25]. The April 2027 MSCI feedback window and the June 2027 decision sit beyond our twelve-month horizon but are the reason the regime can normalise rather than persist. The group injection and placement path is the corporate action to watch: any EMTEK asset sale to SAME or a placement to a strategic holder is a dated event only when announced, and it moves value in either direction [S3,S25].

**KPIs we watch between updates.** Weighted occupancy against 48.1%; revenue per bed and outpatient volume against 729,578 visits; gross margin against 29.7%; capex as a share of revenue against the 7% to 12% path; net debt to EBITDA against 2.2x; the equity-accounted contribution from the JEC associate; and any disclosure on free float or controller sell-down [S3,S4,S5].

bear.narrative: Medical trend keeps running ahead of tariff - BPJS and insurer rates lag cost inflation, so revenue per admission falls as well as volume growing more slowly; the 2025 capacity adds fixed costs, growth runs 4pp slower with gross margin 200bp lower, and insurance panels win a further discount. The JEC associate contributes equity profit only and no dividend uplift.

bull.narrative: The 2025 capacity (Sentul extension, Royal Suites, PET/CT, robotic surgery) fills faster than the base case, complex-case mix lifts revenue per bed, and procurement scale takes gross margin 200bp higher with growth 4pp faster - the mirror of the bear case. KRIS is implemented without a tariff cut for private-class beds. The group also has a documented route to add value - EMTEK took control in 2020 and injected PT Elang Medika Corpora in 2021, and a placement or injection that lifts free float above the exchange minimum is the same playbook.

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-11-11): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S26]

index_deletions.note: 14 Indonesian HSC-category names deleted at the December 2026 review, effective at the open on 21 December 2026

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 revenue of the three reported quarters is running ~9% above the FY2025 base and the LTM to Sep-2026 is above the full FY2025 year, so FY2026E anchors on the run-rate rather than on a haircut; the board states a double-digit growth aspiration for 2026 from the 2025 investments [S3,S4]. FY2027-30 fade to 7% as the 1,428-bed base fills from 48.1% occupancy and KRIS caps inpatient tariff escalation [S3].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchor is the last actual FY2025 gross margin of 29.7% and the 9M-2026 quarters, which hold at ~29.4% despite the 17.8% medical trend rate the company cites for 2026 [S3,S4]. We hold that level and allow only 30bp of procurement and case-mix benefit to FY2030E; no haircut beyond the last actual.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (all-in operating cost, D&A included)
assumptions.basis: EBIT = gross profit less this line, so D&A sits inside it and is added back separately in FCFF. The anchor is the 9M-2026 actual - selling expenses 21.84 + G&A 341.97 less other income 2.31 on revenue 1,532.03 is 23.6% of revenue, and FY2025 was 23.5% [S4,S3]. The earlier 23.0% anchor cited the G&A line alone (22.3%) for a line that also carries selling expense. We start at the actual and allow 80bp of operating leverage to FY2030E as the 2025 capacity matures, with no cost inflation beyond the reported trend.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from LK note 31 to TOTAL D&A - fixed assets Rp231.943bn + right-of-use Rp0.097bn + intangibles Rp21.918bn = Rp253.959bn in FY2025 (13.6% of revenue and Rp232.414bn, 13.6%, in FY2024) [S3]. The data pack's D&A line of Rp76.0bn is roughly a third of the real charge, and EBIT already deducts the intangible amortisation while capex includes intangible additions, so the engine's history add-back and terminal capex must both run at total D&A or FCFF is understated by the amortisation [S0,S3]. We hold the FY2025 total-D&A ratio at 13.6% and let it drift to 12.6% as the asset base grows slower than sales; capex_pct ends at the same 12.6% so the terminal year is at total-D&A parity.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was 18.7% of revenue (Sentul extension, Royal Suites, PET/CT, robotic surgery) but 9M-2026 fixed-asset and intangible additions were only ~6% of revenue as the 2025 build completed [S3,S4]. We model a mid-cycle 7-12% - maintenance at roughly half of D&A plus the announced capacity additions - rather than repeating the 2025 peak. Capex ends at 12.6% of revenue, the same ratio as terminal total D&A (fixed assets plus intangibles), so the terminal year is a maintenance year at total-D&A parity and the base is not run down [S3].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Pack default from the three-year average; receivables from patients and insurers are small relative to revenue and payables fund the drug and consumable book [S0,S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 effective charge was 37% of pre-tax profit because losses at some hospital entities are not recognised against profits elsewhere [S0,S3]; we use 24%, between the 22% statutory rate and the reported effective rate, and above the engine default's 15.5% which is distorted by the FY2023 tax credit.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: HSBC facility priced at JIBOR plus a margin, drawn to fund capex [S3]; with the house BI rate at 5.75% that implies ~8%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Pack default from the three-year average [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 net long-term bank borrowing added ~Rp481bn, largely to fund the Rp412bn additional investment in the JEC associate [S4]; we assume no further net borrowing from FY2026E as capex steps down and operating cash flow covers maintenance.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Engine default constant; the associate's equity-method profit is small and is not consolidated [S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 LK attributes Rp7.4bn of Rp37.5bn net profit, 19.7%, to non-controlling interests, mostly the 20.16% of RSGK that SAME does not own [S3]. We hold that reported share rather than the pack's three-year average, which is lifted by the 2024 minority-heavy year.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend was paid for FY2023 or FY2024 and the AGM resolutions put all profit back into the capacity build [S3]; we assume zero payout through the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Share count has been flat at ~17.16bn since 2022 [S0].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The house long-run nominal growth path for Indonesia, 5%, which a hospital network at 48.1% occupancy on a licensed 1,428-bed base can serve without a new licence or site [S3]. It sits below the medical trend rate the company cites, so the terminal value does not assume the industry's cost inflation is passed through in perpetuity [S3].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check carries 40% of value and is applied to Rp190.29bn, the data pack's LTM EBITDA built from its 76.0 D&A line - the line the report says it does not use. fund record valuation.methods.ev_ebitda.metric = 190.2898, identical to datapack.ltm.ebitda; facts F6/F7 restate only 'da', and the engine rebuilds LTM only if revenue, ebit or np_parent is restated (cov_engine market()), so the restatement never reaches the multiple. On the model's restated FY2025A EBITDA of 346.9 the method gives (11.37 x 346.9 - 650.3) / 17.156 = Rp192; on FY2026E EBITDA of 385.1 it gives Rp217. §4 states the 11.4x is on 'our FY2026E EBITDA' and that the EBITDA 'has already been restated for the true depreciation charge' - both false. At 0.6/0.4 the corrected metric moves the blend from 112 to 154-164, the 12-month value from 103 to 137-146 and the target from 200 to about 267-284, i.e. +13% to +20% against the 236 price: the REDUCE rating is an artefact of this metric error.
challenges.answer: Restated FY2025A revenue (F17), ebit (F18) and np_parent (F19) from the LK, plus ebit FY2024A (F20); the engine now rebuilds LTM so ev_ebitda.metric is the restated 347.6, not the pack's 190.3. Value Rp183, weights 70/30, target 206, REDUCE, and §4 rewritten - the multiple is no longer called a floor.

challenges.challenge: The free-float facts are misstated and miscited. fund record lines 295 and 339 pipe val.konglo.ff.gap_pct through a pct filter and render '85% short of the exchange minimum'; the registry gap is 0.85 percentage points (14.15 vs 15.0, 5.7% relative), so §5 and §6 overstate it 15x. The 15.0% floor and the 31-Mar-2029 deadline are cited to S5, but S5 (4,669 chars, the ANTARA HSC/IHSG piece) contains neither 'float' nor '2029' - zero hits; the rule and the date live in the konglo registry (S25), which the report never cites. The 2029 date also depends on the tier 'mcap below Rp5tn': at about Rp291/share (Rp5.0tn, +23%) the name leaves the small-cap tier and the deck's 12.5-15% band deadline becomes 31 Mar 2027 - and the bull case is Rp290.
challenges.answer: Gap now written as {{val.konglo.ff.gap_pct|pctv}} (0.8pp) not 85%; the 15% rule and both deadlines are cited to S25, the konglo registry snapshot registered for this ticker; the mcap tier is stated and a re-rating is noted as shortening the clock to 2027.

challenges.challenge: The 33.98% JEC stake is marked at LK carrying value Rp849.4bn (S4 p.3, investment in associate 849,429,370,260) in the DCF bridge and netted out of the EV/EBITDA bridge, with no mark test. JECX.JK is covered in this house: house fundamental Rp621/share against a Rp935 price (mcap Rp3,041.8bn). The konglo card requires a covered listed sibling to be marked at its house fundamental pre-lens, which here is 33.98% x about Rp2,020bn = about Rp686bn - Rp163bn (Rp9.5/share, 7.4% of the Rp128 DCF) below the book mark, while the market mark (about Rp1,034bn) is 1.51x house value, exactly the sibling premium the card forbids importing. §4 also misdescribes the mechanics: the stake is not 'carried inside the balance-sheet value used by the model', it is a discrete bridge item. §6 concedes carrying value and market price differ but never quantifies either.
challenges.answer: The 33.98% JEC stake is marked to the house fundamental pre-lens as one bridge item (-162.9), not at the Rp849.4bn LK carrying value (F23); §4 states the book/house/market range and that the mark lowers the DCF, and post_bs_review says so.

challenges.challenge: The group capital-markets upside is absent. EMTEK took 71.88% in Nov 2020 and injected 99.9999% of PT Elang Medika Corpora into SAME in Aug 2021 (S3 p.25) - the documented precedent for SAME as the group's healthcare platform, which §1 says it is. The konglo card names asset injections and spin-offs as the modal rally driver, yet the report mentions the group only as a governance fact and reduces the float agenda to a rights issue or sell-down that 'changes the per-share math' (down). A second upside is unmodelled: the 2025 additions are already capitalised and capex falls to 7%, so filling 1,428 beds from 48.1% occupancy drops through at roughly full conversion to FCFF.
challenges.answer: The 2020 takeover and August 2021 injection of PT Elang Medika Corpora are now a sourced second upside in §5 with the 31 Mar 2029 float deadline; it is in the bull narrative and dated watch items, not in the base case because nothing is announced [S3,S25].

challenges.challenge: Pledged shares are unresolved and the ownership block is unreconciled. §6 says 'we found no pledged-share disclosure ... checked-but-thin' with no source for the negative; S3 (1,130,468 chars) returns zero hits for 'gadai' and 'diagunkan', and the konglo registry carries no pledge field - a registry gap the card says to report, not paper over. The ownership numbers also cannot be read together: EMTEK 79.0% direct (F14), insider 89.01% and free float 14.15% (pack) sum to 103%. For a report whose entire thesis is the float, who holds the other ~10% is load-bearing.
challenges.answer: §6 states that the annual report and Q3 LK were searched for gadai/diagunkan/dijaminkan with no pledged-stake disclosure, reports the missing registry pledge field to the Director, and reconciles 79.0/89.01/14.15 as a definitional overlap it cannot close from the filings [S3,S4,S0].

challenges.challenge: Terminal capital intensity contradicts the growth rate, and the healthcare/compounder card's tests are missing. FY2035E capex is 10.0% of revenue against D&A of 11.5% - net investment minus Rp56bn - while FCFF grows 4% forever; an asset base cannot shrink while revenue compounds. Setting terminal capex at D&A parity cuts terminal FCFF from 256.6 to 200.4 and the DCF from Rp128 to about Rp108 (-16%). On the model's FY2035E, NOPAT of about Rp205 (EBIT 269.7 at 24%) on capital employed of about Rp3.76tn (equity 4,542.5 less net cash 778.9) is a ~5% ROIC against a 10.6% WACC, yet the report states no reinvestment rate, no ROIIC and no implied exit EV/EBIT (14.9x at TV against 21.8x today on FY2026E EBIT), all of which the card requires.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex is set to D&A parity (11.5% of revenue) and the DCF now charges it; §4 states the terminal year is maintenance-only, the reinvestment rate is low and the occupancy fill, not new capital, serves the 5% terminal growth [S3].

challenges.challenge: The scenarios do not match the risk register. KRIS/medical-trend compression is labelled 'high likelihood, high impact' and 'the single most likely way this thesis is wrong', yet it carries only a 25% bear probability with a -150bp gross-margin and -3pp growth shock, and no cut to revenue per admission or to private-tariff revenue. If it is the most likely failure the bear must weigh at least 40%, or the register language must come down. Separately, the 40%-weighted EV/EBITDA uses an LTM metric that is identical across all three scenarios, so 40% of the value is scenario-invariant: bear v0 80.1 against base 112.2 is a 29% spread for a business at 2.4x net debt/EBITDA.
challenges.answer: Bear weight raised to 30% (base 45, bull 25) and the bear shock widened to -4pp growth and -200bp margin, a revenue-per-admission shock mirrored in the bull; §5 now states the multiple is scenario-invariant because it stays on last-actual EBITDA.

challenges.challenge: Two unjustified conservatisms and one incomplete restatement. (a) Terminal growth of 4% sits 100bp below the house 5% nominal-GDP path with no licence or capacity constraint cited (48.1% occupancy on 1,428 beds); 4% to 5% raises the DCF about 14% (Rp128 to about Rp146), partly offsetting C6. (b) Note 31 total D&A is Rp253.958bn for FY2025 (fixed assets 231.943 + intangibles 21.918 + ROU 0.097) and Rp232.128bn for FY2024, but F6/F7 carry only 231.943/212.293 - so §3's claim that the pack 'carries D&A of 231.9bn, which is the LK's fixed-asset depreciation note of 232bn plus intangible amortisation' is wrong on its face (231.9 excludes amortisation), and FY2025A EBITDA is shown at 18.6% against a true 19.8%. (c) For balance, unjustified optimism: tax 24% against 36.8% paid (pbt 59.3, tax 21.8), and a minority share of 31.05% against the FY2025A actual of 7.39/37.46 = 19.7%, a pack default that lowers np_parent/EPS/ROE with no source.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth is 5% on the house path; the §3 sentence now says the LK prints fixed-asset depreciation (F6/F7) with intangible amortisation on its own line (F21) and no total, so the da fact carries the fixed-asset line and EBITDA is conservative; minority share is the reported FY2025 19.7% (F22) [S3].

challenges.challenge: §4 says 'the reverse DCF shows a 16.0% gap between the value creation the current price capitalises and what our forecast delivers'. The engine's reverse_dcf returns target a.revenue_growth, period FY2027E, implied_value 0.1598 on a 0.09 input: 15.98% is the implied growth rate at today's price, not a gap. The gap is about 7pp of revenue growth, and 'a 16.0% gap' is a percentage of nothing.
challenges.answer: §4 now reports the reverse DCF in growth terms - the price needs FY2027E growth of {{rev.implied_value|pct}} against our {{rev.factor|pct}} - instead of calling 16% a gap [engine].

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-capital build does not reproduce its own number: 7.45% + 0.875 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 13.3%, not the 11.7% quoted; the missing -1.62% sovereign default spread (val.coc.default_spread) is never disclosed. The assumptions file also sets cost_of_debt 8.0% (JIBOR plus margin) while §4 quotes 9.45% pre-tax debt, and the model charges interest at 8.0% (FY2026E 78.3 on 978 = 8.0%): two debt costs in one model, neither reconciled.
challenges.answer: §4 shows the full COE build including the {{val.coc.default_spread|pct}} sovereign default-spread deduction, and reconciles the 9.4% WACC debt cost (risk-free plus corporate spread) with the 8.0% contractual facility rate that drives interest expense [S0,S3].

challenges.challenge: Only two methods carry value (dcf 0.60, ev_ebitda 0.40) against the industry default 0.60/0.30/0.10, and the house requires primary plus two cross-checks. The stated reason for dropping P/E (134x on a 1.6% margin) is fair, but the QC gate weights.changed is left unjustified in fund record qc_justifications, and a cheap third cross-check is meaningful here: peers' P/BV against the stock's 1.06x, which tests the report's own 'book value is large relative to profit' claim and the 0.8% ROE.
challenges.answer: Weights are now 70% DCF and 30% EV/EBITDA with a qc_justifications entry for weights.changed explaining why P/E and P/BV carry no information at a 1.6% net margin, an 0.9% ROE and a revalued book [S3].

missing_bull_case.note: No group capital-markets upside despite the documented EMTEK precedent (71.88% in Nov 2020, then 99.9999% of EMC injected into SAME in Aug 2021, S3 p.25), and no value shown for filling 1,428 beds from 48.1% occupancy now that the 2025 build is capitalised and capex falls to 7%.

missing_bear_case.note: Pledged shares unresolved (zero hits for gadai/diagunkan in 1.13m chars of S3; no pledge field in the konglo registry); the JEC associate is marked at book 849.4 against a covered sibling's house fundamental of ~686; and KRIS is called high likelihood yet carries only 25%.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue growth 10% is well anchored (9M26 +12.0% YoY) and gross margin 29.4% is defensible, but terminal capex 10% sits below D&A 11.5% while FCFF grows 4% forever, and the EV/EBITDA metric is not the EBITDA the report says it is.

evidence_and_citations.note: S5 is cited three times for the 15.0% free-float floor and the 31-Mar-2029 deadline but contains neither 'float' nor '2029' (4,669 chars); the rendered report says '85% short of the exchange minimum' for a 0.85pp gap; §3's '231.9bn ... plus intangible amortisation' contradicts note 31 (total 253.958).

valuation_method_fit.note: Fatal metric error in the 40%-weighted EV/EBITDA (pack LTM 190.3, not restated 346.9/385.1); only two methods and the weights.changed WARN unanswered; associate marked at book with no house-value test; no reinvestment/ROIC or implied exit-multiple test; terminal capex < D&A.

bias_and_tone.note: The REDUCE is driven by one heroic input pointing down - a multiple value of 88 that on the report's own stated metric would be 217 - and the prose calls that 88 'the floor a trade buyer would anchor to'. The float gap is overstated 15x in two sections.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: HSC status, the IHSG exclusion of 13 Nov 2026 and the FTSE deletion of 21 Dec 2026 are read correctly and S6 does name SAME, but the free-float tier (mcap below Rp5tn, ~Rp291/share) is never stated, so the 2027-vs-2029 deadline cliff - and the registry's empty group field for an EMTEK-controlled name - go unflagged.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: terminal g 4% vs the house 5% path (+14% DCF) and a D&A restatement that omits 21.9bn amortisation + 0.1bn ROU, leaving FY2025A EBITDA at 18.6% vs a true 19.8%. Unjustified optimism: tax 24% vs 36.8% paid; minority share 31.05% vs 19.7% actual. Business scenarios are mirrored (+/-3pp growth, +/-150bp GM) and base is 50%, so no asymmetry there.

calibration.note: Gate passes: FY2026E EBITDA margin 18.80% vs FY2025A 18.63%, gap 0.17pp, and FY2026E revenue 2,048 is 1.0% above the 2,026.7 LTM to Sep-2026. No BLOCK flags. The pass is on a history whose D&A base is narrower than note 31 (C8), not on a wrong FY+1.

signoff.notes: Approved on the valuation. Rebuilt: DCF 99 + 12.4x x 369.7 EV/EBITDA 220 = blend 135 -> base 151; weighted 155 less 20% liquidity = fundamental 124; konglo lens keeps 1.688 (base 35% = deck 30% + 5pp HSC, bear 75%, bull -10%) -> target 210, -11.1%. JEC associate marked at the house fundamental of the covered sibling pre-lens (686.5 vs LK 849.4, market ~1,034) per the konglo card; JECX is a house SELL. Lens and konglo profile present in §4, §5 and §6 with {{table:konglo}}; registry facts match S25/S26 (HSC 11 Nov, IHSG out 13 Nov, FTSE out 21 Dec 2026, float 14.15% vs 15.0%, next step 31 Mar 2029, mcap 4.05tn below the 5tn tier so no ff_deadline flag). REDUCE is right and not a batch tilt: it matches PRAY, the other konglo hospital name (REDUCE, -14.8%); the SELLs are non-konglo or extreme-premium names. Five open FIX do not touch FCFF or the target: Q11 changes only the FY2026E interest/net-profit line (~26.6 -> ~7) and the leverage path; Q10/Q12/Q13/Q14 are §3/§4/§5 text. Clear at the next refresh, Q13 (CFO 340.1 vs profit 37.5, accruals ~-5.3%) first because it inverts the house earnings-quality conclusion. New text note: the §4 sentence 'Rp203 before the HSC overlay; the overlay adds 5%' is mechanically wrong - 203 already includes the 5pp HSC adjustment and 210 is the probability-weighted mean of 150/203/284. Q15-Q18 open; 24% tax vs 37% effective is worth ~Rp6/sh and does not change REDUCE. No broker/consensus contamination in report, sources or peer set.

bias.note: Base 45% with a mirrored bear/bull (+/-4pp growth, +/-200bp gross margin) and terminal g 5% on the house path. Drivers sit on the last actual or the 9M filing: gross margin 29.4% vs 29.7%/29.4% actual, opex 23.6% = 9M actual, da_pct 13.6% = the note-31 total, capex 7% vs 9M additions of 5.7% of revenue [S3,S4]. No default haircuts, no unsourced volume decline. Mild optimisms (24% tax vs the 37% FY2025 effective charge; 80bp opex leverage; 12.6% long-run capex) are argued in the assumptions file; mild conservatisms (FY2026E growth 10% vs 9M +12.0%, gross margin held flat) offset. Net: neutral.

findings.finding: The §3 restatement paragraph double counts and mislabels note 31. It reads 'fixed-asset depreciation of {{fact.F6|num1}}bn for FY2025 and {{fact.F7|num1}}bn for FY2024, plus right-of-use depreciation and intangible amortisation of {{fact.F21|num1}}bn on the next line' and so prints 254.0 + 21.9 = 276bn; but F6/F7 ARE the totals (231.943 fixed assets + 0.097 ROU + 21.918 intangibles = 253.959, note 31 p.210) and fixed-asset depreciation alone is 231.943. A reader does the subtraction and gets 276bn against the EBITDA-EBIT difference of 254.0 [S3,F6,F21].

Forward debt and interest do not start from the balance sheet the valuation uses. Bank loans plus leases are 1,298.1 at 30 Sep 2026 (100.0 short + 18.4 current + 1,178.9 long + 0.8 leases) against 978.2 at 31 Dec 2025, and the DCF bridge correctly carries net debt 1,122.6 [S4]; yet line.debt opens FY2026E at the FY2025A 978.2 and interest is 78.3 (8% x 978.2), so forecast net debt is 711.5 in FY2026E - a fall from 1,122.6 within one quarter - and interest is understated by ~26bn at the stated 8% cost (np_parent FY2026E 26.6 would be ~7).

The §5 risk register states 'Net debt is 2.2x EBITDA' with no date. 2.2x is FY2025 year-end (825.7/369.7, as §3 correctly dates it); at the model's own balance-sheet date the multiple is 3.0x (1,122.6/369.7) [S4], lifted by the Rp412bn JEC investment. Leverage risk reads lighter than the balance sheet says.

§3's cash-conversion sentence draws the wrong inference and the accruals test is missing. 'Net profit of IDR30.1bn against FCFF of IDR39.7bn means earnings are not yet cash, and the accruals gap closes only if capex falls' - FCFF exceeds net profit, and the FY2025 LK shows operating cash flow of 340.1 against total net profit of 37.5, i.e. accruals of about -5.3% of average assets (FY2024 -4.5%) [S3 pp.6,61]. Earnings are strongly cash-backed; the constraint is capex of 348.4, which is reinvestment, not accruals.

The §4 reverse-DCF comparator is the engine's solved increment, not our forecast: 'against the {{rev.factor|pct}} our forecast delivers' prints 9.5%, while reverse_dcf.factor is 0.094666 - the amount added to the 0.09 FY2027E input to reach the 0.1847 implied. The model's FY2027E growth is 9.0% (2,232.5/2,048.2) and the assumptions file says 0.09.

tax_rate 24% sits below the 37% effective charge the FY2025 LK shows; the non-recognition of losses is a cash tax cost while those entities stay loss-making. On the DCF leg 13pp of tax is worth roughly 6 rupiah a share. The choice is argued, but it runs against the card's 'use the rate the LK shows being paid'.

The compounder card's multiple-survival and owner-earnings tests are asserted, not shown: no implied exit EV/EBIT against the 12.4x entry multiple, and maintenance vs growth capex is described only qualitatively against the 7%-to-12.6% path.

History is half-restated: FY2024A/FY2025A D&A are the note-31 totals (232.4/253.9) but FY2022A/FY2023A remain the pack lines (98.2/88.2), so line EBITDA jumps from ~120 to ~335 at FY2024A. No forecast or published figure depends on it, but a history chart or growth series would mislead.
